newsitem.title: USA: NEA vote new chapter in art agency's rocky history.
newsitem.headline: NEA vote new chapter in art agency's rocky history.

text.p: Friday's House vote on the future of the National Endowment for the Arts (NEA) is the latest chapter in a saga sparked by controversy over a shocking, homoerotic photo of a man with a bullwhip.

The NEA, a $100-million-a-year agency that awards grants to bolster excellence in art and public access to it, ran into a storm of criticism in the 1980's because of avant-garde exhibits that were funded by the public.

Those included the works of the late photographer Robert Mapplethorpe, whose NEA-funded explicit portrait of himself cavorting sexually with a bullwhip became the poster child for conservative critics of publicly funded arts.

Other examples from the debate included "Piss Christ," a photograph of a crucifix suspended in urine, and a depiction of Jesus and Lazarus in a homosexual pose. But the controversial projects -- numbered at less than 40 by the NEA -- were a small minority among the 110,000 funded by the the agency.
Drastic reforms at the NEA have screened out the kind of works that are sure to offend religious groups, but the fight is far from done.

"I don't think this is over yet," NEA Chairwoman Jane Alexander told Reuters on Friday after the House voted 271-155 to reject a plan that would have parceled out NEA funding to the states in the form of block grants.
Such a plan would have meant the end of the 32-year-old NEA as it included $10 million in funding aimed at permanantly shutting the NEA's doors.

On Thursday, the House voted 217-216 to dismantle the NEA, but the Senate and the White House are widely expected to rescue it. President Bill Clinton has threatened to veto the entire $13 billion Interior Department appropriations bill if the agency is gutted.

The NEA has powerful enemies in the Republican-controlled House and Senate, including such Republican leaders as House Speaker Newt Gingrich of Georgia, House Majority Leader Dick Armey of Texas and Sen. Jesse Helms of North Carolina.

"There's no place in a democratic society for the government to be determining what is and what is not art," Michele Davis, a spokeswoman for Armey, said on Friday. "It's part of the Washington-knows-best attitude."
Davis acknowledged the NEA has changed since the days of Mapplethorpe, who died of AIDS in 1989, but opponents like Armey believe the government should get out of the arts business altogether.
Alexander, the actress who took over as NEA chairwoman in October 1993, has led a series of changes that allow the NEA to better control the projects it funds.
The NEA now bans grants to individuals except for writers, forbids groups that receive grants to reissue NEA funds to others and requires midterm reports on projects to avoid any embarrassments.
Many of the changes were mandated by Congress, which switched to Republican hands after the 1994 elections.

Until this week's efforts to abolish the NEA, it had been merely the funding that came under attack by opponents. The NEA budget, which reached a high of $176 million in 1992, has been whittled down to the current $99.5 million.
